prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms held at the magic wavelength allow time to be measured with a precision that could not be reached before

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: optical lattice clocks, Katori and Ye, as the whole prize. The chair asked for one sentence on what the lattice clock showed that the 2005 and 2012 prizes did not, and I think it can be given. The comb gave a way to count optical cycles. The 2012 prize gave control of a single quantum system, whose limit is statistics: one ion gives very little signal per unit time. Katori's idea was that at a magic wavelength the trapping light shifts both clock levels equally, so thousands of neutral atoms can be held tightly and interrogated together with the trap perturbation engineered away. That made ion-level systematic accuracy and many-atom statistics available in the same instrument, and it was an unexpected result, since confinement had been thought to ruin an optical transition. Experimentally it has been verified in the way I care about most. Independent laboratories in Japan, the US, Europe and China build their own lattice clocks and their comparisons agree at the 1e-18 level, and the clocks resolve gravitational redshift across millimetres. That is a door opened onto measurements nobody could make before. The credit is the clearest on the shortlist: Katori for the proposal and first strontium realisation, Ye for taking the scheme to the accuracy and many-body frontier. I would keep the citation on the lattice clock itself, not on a record number that will be superseded and not on the comb.
statement.case_against: The distinctness question has not been closed. Danielsson and Eriksson are entitled to say that a better instrument is not automatically a new discovery, and Ye's name already sits in the comb lineage. I think the magic-wavelength condition answers this, but I cannot show it to a sceptic's satisfaction in one line. Two-name credit also leaves out Lemonde, Ludlow, Lemke, Takamoto, Derevianko and Bloom, and I cannot judge from the written record how the original proposal, the first demonstration and the accuracy record should be weighed. The redefinition of the second is still pending. I also have to recognise that topological insulators have broader support (seven of eight rankings, five in the top three), that Kroll, Lindroth and I are all close to precision measurement or atomic physics, and that the first-round tally shows no majority for any single configuration. Support counts do not settle the matter, but a strong, independently confirmed B024 with an unresolved name list is a serious competitor and I would not obstruct it on scientific grounds.

responses.point: Danielsson moved topological insulators to first place, says nature supplying the clue matters to him, and asks for a sharper statement of what the lattice clock showed beyond the comb and ion-clock prizes. He also wrote that the failed graphene realisation shows why the experimental share must carry weight in the B024 citation.
responses.response: I take your challenge on the clock as the right question and I have tried to answer it in my case above: the lattice makes many-atom statistics and ion-level systematics available together, which neither earlier prize delivered, and it was counter-intuitive that a tight optical trap could be made harmless. On your point about B024, I agree that the HgTe observation is why the experimental share matters. That is exactly the standard I apply to the clock, where the experimental demonstration and its independent reproduction are the discovery. I do not accept that a clock is less a measurement of nature than a neutrino flux is. A gravitational redshift resolved across a millimetre is nature answering a question we could not ask before. If you remain unpersuaded on distinctness, I would still ask you to tell the committee whether it is a matter of kind or of degree, because that determines whether you would vote against B001 or only rank it lower.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, argues that Kane and Mele should not be split because they wrote the founding Z2 papers, and names the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and of Hasan as a real cost.
responses.response: I agree with you that Mele should stay with Kane, and I said so in round 1, so on the trio we do not differ. My remaining difficulty is the one you name yourself: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe system that was then measured, and Zhang cannot be credited now. I would be concerned that a three-name B024 prize attributes the experimental discovery to the wrong prediction and leaves a gap that the citation cannot hide. If you wrote the citation around the Z2 invariant and the observation of the quantum spin Hall state, I could support it as my second choice, but I cannot make it my first as long as three people have to stand in for a field with at least six defensible claimants. For clocks the claimants outside Katori and Ye are real but they are contributors to a result whose two decisive steps are clear.

responses.point: Johansson prefers Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, saying that without Hasan the prize honours a prediction and one experiment in a narrow system, and that dropping Hasan leaves the 3D discovery unrecognised.
responses.response: I thought about this seriously, and I am still not persuaded that the 3D step can be placed in the same discovery on the written record. The 3D observation followed the Fu-Kane and Moore-Balents predictions, so including Hasan while leaving out Fu, Moore and Balents creates a new gap in order to fill another. At the same time I accept your cost as real: with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp the 3D class of materials is left unmentioned, and the citation would have to say honestly that the prize is for the quantum spin Hall effect. Both of your trio and mine seem to me defensible but neither is clean, and that is my main reason for not making B024 the lead. I also note and respect that you have set your own circuit QED preference aside because of your disclosed Chalmers connection.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, pairs B001 with B021 (IceCube, Halzen alone), but acknowledges that the single-name IceCube credit is the weakest link and that he would prefer B024 as the main prize if a fair allocation exists.
responses.response: I appreciate that you identified the B021 attribution as your weakest point, and I agree with it. A single name for a cubic-kilometre detector built by hundreds of people, with AMANDA and DUMAND before it, is a credit I could not defend to the public or in the committee, and your configuration would add it to a clock prize that is already complete with two names. I do not think adding a second achievement improves a prize when it adds a credit dispute. I would ask you to consider whether your support for B001 can stand alone: you have written that the clock science and its two-name credit are sound, and you and I hold that view jointly. A two-part prize would only be better than B001 alone if the second part were as clean as the first, and for IceCube I do not think it is.

responses.point: Lindroth supports lattice clocks with a citation about the invention and realisation rather than a record number, and notes that a record will be broken while the principle will not.
responses.response: I agree entirely, and I would turn it into a recommendation for the final ballot: the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice or the optical lattice clock itself, say nothing about the 1e-18 figure as a prize-winning achievement, and avoid practical-impact language since the second has not been redefined. I would also keep our disclosures in view. You and Kroll are closer to the field than I am, and I do not treat our agreement as an independent confirmation of the scientific case. The agreement across the independent laboratories is the evidence that counts.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the magic-wavelength lattice clock as a distinct discovery or as an extension of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; this is the main factor that could move me.
Whether the omission of Lemonde, Ludlow, Lemke, Takamoto and Derevianko is acceptable in a two-name prize, and how the original proposal, first demonstration and accuracy record should be weighed.

Whether topological insulators can be given a defensible three-name allocation given Mele versus Hasan and the absence of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang; if the committee finds a trio it can accept, B024 would be my first alternative and I would accept it as the prize.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should lead the committee to wait or to recognise the achievement now.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with Katori, Ye or any other credited name: I have no recorded co-authorship, institutional tie or supervision relation with any of them. The shared Chalmers environment with Johansson, whose circuit QED preference is only an alternative, and with Mehlig at Gothenburg is institutional only. I note, as other members have, that Kroll and Lindroth are close to precision measurement and atomic physics, and that I am an experimentalist in a different field, so our agreement on B001 should not be counted as independent confirmation. My opening ranking placed B001 first, and I have disclosed that ranking in this record.
